Tunisian Dinar Plunges as Currency Crisis Deepens, Utilities and Businesses Struggle

Tunisia’s economy is facing mounting turmoil as the national currency, the dinar, has seen a precipitous decline against the euro and US dollar, sparking widespread concern among businesses and households. The currency crisis, which began to accelerate in late May, intensified this week as the central bank’s foreign reserves dipped to their lowest levels since 2011.

The sharp devaluation has triggered immediate repercussions across key sectors. Societe Tunisienne de l'Electricite et du Gaz (STEG), the country’s state-run utility provider, reported significant difficulties in paying for imported fuel and equipment. “Our cost of imports has surged by more than 35% in just two months,” said a STEG spokesperson. “This threatens our ability to maintain stable electricity and gas supply, especially during peak summer demand.”

According to the Tunisian Union of Industry and Commerce, over 70% of manufacturers reliant on imported raw materials have either reduced production or temporarily halted operations. Retailers across Tunis and Sfax have reported shortages of basic goods, as importers struggle to secure foreign currency and suppliers raise prices in response to the dinar’s slide.

The government has pledged to protect vulnerable households and ensure essential services remain operational, but economists warn that the crisis may worsen without external support. “The currency collapse is feeding into runaway inflation, eroding purchasing power and risking social unrest,” said local analyst Asma Ben Youssef. Inflation reached 13.4% in May, the highest in over two decades.

With IMF negotiations stalled and investor confidence shaken, the outlook remains uncertain. “We need urgent structural reforms and international assistance,” said Finance Minister Samir El Fekih at a press briefing. Meanwhile, consumers and businesses wait anxiously as Tunisia’s economic crisis continues to unfold.
